The two routes give the same lineshape. SimpCalc leaves the carrier at 0 Hz unless you set variable_offset and variable_ref (as simulate_spectrum does for you), so with a narrow sw the peak can sit away from the centre of the window.

docs.title: From DFT to an NMR spectrum
docs.text:
This guide takes you from a DFT calculation (CASTEP .magres or VASP OUTCAR) to a simulated solid-state NMR spectrum. The main tool is simulate_spectrum(), which chooses sensible simulation settings for you.

Requires SIMPSON

Cells that call simulate_spectrum() or SimpCalc.run() need the simpson command on your PATH (see Installation). The outputs shown on this page were produced with SIMPSON 6.1.4, available on Gitlab.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text: The first cell downloads the example files used on this page from the SimPYson repository. Skip it if you are using your own files.

docs.title: What simulate_spectrum does by default
docs.text: Everything you do not specify is filled in from a set of defaults. To see exactly what was sent to SIMPSON, keep the input file with filepath= and delete_files=False, then print its par block:

docs.title: Automatic choices
docs.text:
Three things are worked out from the spin system, so that the peaks sit in the middle of the spectrum without you computing anything.

What How it is chosen Spectral width sw Twice the spread of the isotropic shifts (at least 10 ppm), rounded up to a whole multiple of spin_rate for MAS, so spinning sidebands fold onto the peaks. With a quadrupole interaction and the central transition detected (Inc), it is \(C_Q^2/\nu_\mathrm{L}\) instead (the second-order broadening); with only quadrupolar interactions and no shifts it uses the same formula, or \(2.5\,C_Q\) when not detecting the central transition. Carrier variable_offset and reference variable_ref The carrier is put at the centre of the shift range and the reference is set so that the axis reads in Hz relative to the transmitter frequency. This is why a single peak at 100 ppm is still centred. Detected operator Inc (central transition) for any quadrupolar nucleus with spin = n/2, where n=1, 3, 5, 7, and 9, unless you specify a diferent detect_operator.

If the spin system has neither shift nor quadrupole lines, there is nothing to estimate from and you must pass sw yourself.

The cell below runs four tiny simulations and prints what was chosen for each:

docs.title: Overriding the defaults
docs.text: Pass any parameter as a keyword. Here, a lower field, faster spinning, narrower lines and interpolation by zero-filling:

docs.title: Shielding to chemical shift
docs.text:
The usual DFT pitfall

DFT gives the magnetic shielding \(\sigma\). SIMPSON needs the chemical shift \(\delta\), the quantity you compare with experiment. Soprano converts one into the other with

\[ \delta = \frac{\sigma_\mathrm{ref} + m\,\sigma}{1 - \sigma_\mathrm{ref} \times 10^{-6}} \]

where \(\sigma_\mathrm{ref}\) is ref and \(m\) is grad. If you leave ref out, Soprano raises an warning. If you use a wrong value, the spectrum is shifted by the same amount without any warning.

  • ref is specific to your calculation (code, functional, pseudopotentials, geometry) and to the nucleus. A value taken from a different setup shifts every peak.
  • grad is normally close to \(-1\). Soprano warns for values outside \(-1.5\) to \(-0.5\).
  • The two values on this page (31.7 for 1H in ethanol; 31P and 27Al for AlPO-14 below) belong to the calculations in the example files. Do not reuse them for your own data.
  • Check the result against something you know: a reference compound computed with the same settings, or a peak position from experiment.

docs.title: VASP calculations
docs.text: A VASP OUTCAR stores the shielding and electric field gradient in units that Soprano and SIMPSON cannot use directly, and ASE does not attach them to the structure. read_vasp parses the file and returns an ASE Atoms object with the ms and efg arrays, just like a .magres file:

docs.title: Large or quadrupolar systems
docs.text:
AlPO-14 contains eight 27Al and eight 31P sites per cell. SIMPSON builds one density matrix for the whole spin system, and its dimension is the product of the number of states, 2I+1, of every nucleus. For eight 27Al (I = 5/2, six states each) this gives \(6^8 \approx 1.7\) million, which is not computable in most machines. Eight 31P, which is much smaller, but with the default powder average (rep2000, 16 gamma angles) still requires some compute time and memory.

When the sites do not interact (no dipolar or J couplings in the spin system, as here), you do not need to simulate them together. Simulate one site at a time and add the spectra: the sum is the same spectrum for a fraction of the cost.

The function below does that for any element of a structure. For the quadrupolar 27Al, q_order=2 adds the second-order quadrupolar interaction, and simulate_spectrum automatically detects the central transition (Inc) and sizes the spectral width from \(C_Q\).

docs.title: The same thing with SimpCalc
docs.text: simulate_spectrum is a thin layer over SimpCalc. If you want to fix every setting yourself, or keep the SIMPSON input file to run on a cluster, build the calculation explicitly. This is one 27Al site with all parameters spelled out (note that SimpCalc has no defaults for these and raises an error if one is missing):

docs.title: Custom simulations with SimpCalc
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from simpyson import SimpCalc

spinsys = """
channels 13C
nuclei 13C 13C
shift 1 50p 0 0 0 0 0
shift 2 20p 0 0 0 0 0
"""

calc = SimpCalc(
    spinsys,
    pulse_sequence="pulse_90",
    proton_frequency=400e6,  # Hz
    spin_rate=10e3,  # Hz
    start_operator="Inz",
    detect_operator="Inp",
    method="direct",
    crystal_file="rep100",
    gamma_angles=10,
    np=4096,
    sw=20e3,  # Hz
    verbose=0,
    lb=10,
    zerofill=4096,
)
calc.print()

spinsys {
channels 13C
nuclei 13C 13C
shift 1 50p 0 0 0 0 0
shift 2 20p 0 0 0 0 0
}

par {
   crystal_file         rep100
   detect_operator      Inp
   gamma_angles         10
   method               direct
   np                   4096
   proton_frequency     400000000.0
   spin_rate            10000.0
   start_operator       Inz
   sw                   20000.0
   verbose              0
   variable num_channels    1
   variable pH              5.0
   variable phH             90
   variable plH             50000
   variable tsw             1e6/sw
}


proc pulseq {} {
    global par
    pulse $par(pH) $par(plH) $par(phH)
    acq_block {
        delay $par(tsw)
    }
}


proc main {} {
    global par
    set f [fsimpson]
    faddlb $f 10 0
    fzerofill $f 4096
    fft $f
    fsave $f $par(name).spe
}



result = calc.run()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), constrained_layout=True)
ax[0].plot(result.fid["time"], result.fid["real"])
ax[0].set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
ax[0].set_title("FID")
ax[1].plot(result.spe["ppm"], result.spe["real"])
ax[1].set_xlim(100, 0)
ax[1].set_xlabel("$^{13}$C (ppm)")
ax[1].set_title("Spectrum")
plt.show()

from simpyson.templates import pulseq_templates

for name, template in pulseq_templates.items():
    instance = template()
    print(f"{name}: {instance.description}")
    for parameter, value in instance.get_default_parameters().items():
        print(f"    {parameter.removeprefix('variable_'):<14} {value!r}")

no_pulse: No pulse, direct acquisition
    tsw            '1e6/sw'
    offset         0.0
    num_channels   1
pulse_90: Single 90° pulse on 1H
    pH             5.0
    plH            50000
    phH            '90'
    tsw            '1e6/sw'
    num_channels   1
cp_mas: Cross-polarization magic angle spinning
    pcp            1000
    plHcp          70000
    phHcp          '0'
    plCcp          69000
    phCcp          '0'
    dw             '1e6/spin_rate/gamma_angles'
Template What it does Notes 'no_pulse' Acquire only. Start from a transverse operator (Inx). offset sets the carrier in Hz (simulate_spectrum uses this template). 'pulse_90' One pulse on the first channel, then acquire. Defaults: 5 µs at 50 kHz (a 90° pulse), phase 90. Other channels get zero power. Start from Inz. 'cp_mas' Cross-polarisation contact pulse, then acquisition with the dipolar and J couplings turned off. Needs channels 1H 13C in that order. Start from I1x. pcp is in µs, plHcp/plCcp are rf powers in Hz.

All durations are in microseconds and all rf powers in Hz. The default tsw and dw are Tcl expressions evaluated by SIMPSON from sw, spin_rate and gamma_angles.

A misspelled template name is not an error

Any string that is not a template name is treated as your own Tcl code. pulse_sequence="pulse90" does not raise; it produces an input file with the text pulse90 inside the pulse sequence. Use calc.print() to check what was generated.

half = SimpCalc(
    spinsys,
    pulse_sequence="pulse_90",
    pH=2.5,  # pulse length in microseconds (default 5.0)
    proton_frequency=400e6,
    spin_rate=10e3,
    start_operator="Inz",
    detect_operator="Inp",
    method="direct",
    crystal_file="rep100",
    gamma_angles=10,
    np=4096,
    sw=20e3,
    verbose=0,
)
print([line.strip() for line in half.generate_par().splitlines() if "variable" in line])

['variable num_channels    1', 'variable pH              2.5', 'variable phH             90', 'variable plH             50000', 'variable tsw             1e6/sw']

There are two other ways, which give the same result:

  • Build the template yourself and pass the object: SimpCalc(spinsys, pulse_sequence=Pulse90(pH=2.5), ...). This is fine for single-channel spin systems; with several channels, use the name instead, because only the name route tells the template how many channels there are (otherwise SIMPSON stops with pulse: arguments must match number of channels).
  • Change a template that is already attached to a calculator with calc.pulse_sequence.update_parameters(pH=2.5). This is handy for scanning a parameter, see below.

Internally, template parameters are stored with a variable_ prefix, which is how they appear in the par block (variable pH 2.5). Always give them without the prefix: variable_pH=2.5 passed to SimpCalc together with a template name is ignored and the default is kept.

cp_spinsys = """
channels 1H 13C
nuclei 1H 13C 13C
shift 1 2.0p 0 0 0 0 0
shift 2 10p 0 0 0 0 0
shift 3 15p 0 0 0 0 0
dipole 1 2 -10000 0 0 0
dipole 1 3 -5000 0 0 0
"""

cp_calc = SimpCalc(
    cp_spinsys,
    pulse_sequence="cp_mas",
    proton_frequency=400e6,
    sw=20e3,
    spin_rate=10e3,
    start_operator="I1x",
    detect_operator="I2p+I3p",
    method="direct",
    crystal_file="rep100",
    gamma_angles=10,
    verbose=0,
    np=4096,
    lb=20,
)

cp_calc.pulse_sequence.update_parameters(pcp=1000)  # 1 ms contact time
sim_short = cp_calc.run()

cp_calc.pulse_sequence.update_parameters(pcp=8000)  # 8 ms contact time
sim_long = cp_calc.run()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), constrained_layout=True)

ax.plot(
    sim_short.spe["ppm"],
    sim_short.spe["real"] / sim_short.spe["real"].max(),
    label="Short contact time (1000 µs)",
)
ax.plot(
    sim_long.spe["ppm"],
    sim_long.spe["real"] / sim_long.spe["real"].max() + 1,
    label="Long contact time (8000 µs)",
)
ax.axvline(10, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.5)
ax.axvline(15, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Chemical shift (ppm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Normalised intensity")
ax.set_xlim(20, 5)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Effect of CP contact time on the $^{13}$C spectrum")
plt.show()

tcl = """
pulse $par(pw) $par(rf) 90
acq_block {
    delay $par(tsw)
}
"""

pulse_spinsys = "channels 13C\nnuclei 13C\nshift 1 20p 0 0 0 0 0\n"

custom = SimpCalc(
    pulse_spinsys,
    pulse_sequence=tcl,
    pw=2.5,
    rf=100e3,
    tsw="1e6/sw",  # values for the $par(...) placeholders
    proton_frequency=400e6,
    spin_rate=10e3,
    start_operator="Inz",
    detect_operator="Inp",
    method="direct",
    crystal_file="rep100",
    gamma_angles=10,
    np=1024,
    sw=20e3,
    verbose=0,
)
custom.print()

spinsys {
channels 13C
nuclei 13C
shift 1 20p 0 0 0 0 0
}

par {
   crystal_file         rep100
   detect_operator      Inp
   gamma_angles         10
   method               direct
   np                   1024
   proton_frequency     400000000.0
   spin_rate            10000.0
   start_operator       Inz
   sw                   20000.0
   verbose              0
   variable pw              2.5
   variable rf              100000.0
   variable tsw             1e6/sw
}


proc pulseq {} {
    global par

pulse $par(pw) $par(rf) 90
acq_block {
    delay $par(tsw)
}

}


proc main {} {
    global par
    set f [fsimpson]
    faddlb $f 20 0
    fzerofill $f 1024
    fft $f
    fsave $f $par(name).spe
}

How the placeholders are handled:

  • Every $par(name) in the code needs a value. If one is missing, SimpCalc raises ValueError: Missing required parameters: ... straight away.
  • Names that are standard SimpCalc parameters (spin_rate, sw, np, ...) can be used as $par(spin_rate) without being repeated.
  • A keyword argument that matches no $par(...) is not passed to the pulse sequence. It is still written into the par block as a plain entry, so a typo does not raise an error either.
  • Values can be numbers or Tcl expressions given as strings (tsw="1e6/sw"). The variable lines are written in alphabetical order, so an expression can only refer to a variable that sorts before it.
  • If your code starts with proc pulseq, it is used as it is and nothing is added. This lets you define helper procedures (see below).

Change a value between runs with update_parameters. For example, a nutation curve: the signal after one pulse against the pulse length.

pulse_lengths = np.linspace(0.25, 10, 40)  # microseconds
signal = []
for pw in pulse_lengths:
    custom.pulse_sequence.update_parameters(pw=float(pw))
    signal.append(custom.run().fid["real"][0])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), constrained_layout=True)
ax.plot(pulse_lengths, signal, "o-")
ax.set_xlabel("Pulse length (µs)")
ax.set_ylabel("Signal (first FID point)")
ax.set_title("Nutation at 100 kHz rf")
plt.show()

The signal is maximal at 2.5 µs, a 90° pulse at 100 kHz (\(1/(4\,\nu_1)\)), and zero at 5 µs (180°).

ramped_cp = """
proc pulseq {} {
    global par
    set tr [expr 1e6/$par(spin_rate)]
    set ntr [expr round($par(tcp)/$tr)]
    set tau [expr $ntr*$tr]
    ramp $tau $par(ramp_start) $par(ramp_stop) $par(steps) $par(rf_H) $par(rf_C)
    acq_block {
        delay $par(dw)
    }
}

proc ramp {tau start stop steps rfH rfC} {
    set dt [expr $tau/$steps]
    for {set i 1} {$i <= $steps} {incr i} {
        set per_amp [expr $start+($i*($stop-$start)/$steps)]
        set amp [expr $rfH*$per_amp/100]
        pulse $dt $amp 0 $rfC 0
    }
}
"""

offsets = np.arange(
    -16, 17, 2
)  # change of the 1H power (kHz) around the n = 1 match, 60 kHz


def intensity(result):
    """Summed intensity of the 10 ppm carbon (the strongly coupled one)."""
    ppm, real = result.spe["ppm"], result.spe["real"]
    return real[np.abs(ppm - 10) < 3].sum()


def run_flat(rf_H):
    cp_calc.pulse_sequence.update_parameters(pcp=2000, plHcp=rf_H, plCcp=70e3)
    return intensity(cp_calc.run())


def run_ramp(rf_H, start):
    ramp_calc = SimpCalc(
        cp_spinsys,
        pulse_sequence=ramped_cp,
        tcp=2000,
        ramp_start=start,
        ramp_stop=100,
        steps=20,
        rf_H=rf_H,
        rf_C=70e3,
        dw="1e6/spin_rate/gamma_angles",
        proton_frequency=400e6,
        spin_rate=10e3,
        start_operator="I1x",
        detect_operator="I2p+I3p",
        method="direct",
        crystal_file="rep100",
        gamma_angles=10,
        np=4096,
        sw=20e3,
        verbose=0,
        lb=20,
    )
    return intensity(ramp_calc.run())


flat = np.array([run_flat(60e3 + d * 1e3) for d in offsets])
ramp_20 = np.array([run_ramp(60e3 + d * 1e3, 80) for d in offsets])
ramp_70 = np.array([run_ramp(60e3 + d * 1e3, 30) for d in offsets])

best = flat[offsets == 0][0]  # flat contact exactly on the match
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), constrained_layout=True)
ax.plot(offsets, flat / best, "o-", label="flat (cp_mas)")
ax.plot(offsets, ramp_20 / best, "s-", label="ramp 80 → 100 % (20 %)")
ax.plot(offsets, ramp_70 / best, "^-", label="ramp 30 → 100 % (70 %)")
ax.axvline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Offset of the $^1$H rf power from the match (kHz)")
ax.set_ylabel("Intensity relative to a matched flat contact")
ax.set_title("Hartmann-Hahn mismatch, 2 ms contact")
ax.set_ylim(0, 2.0)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()

The flat contact is best right on a match, at 0 kHz, and at −10 kHz, where the proton power of 50 kHz is the \(n = 2\) condition. A few kHz away it falls to a fraction of that, and at +10 kHz, where both channels have the same power, it transfers nothing. The 20 % ramp gives less than the flat contact at 0 kHz, because the match lies at the very end of its sweep. Whenever the match lies inside its range (−8 to −4 kHz and +4 to +12 kHz) it transfers 1.2 to 1.5 times as much as the matched flat contact. The 70 % ramp has a lower maximum, but gives 0.8 to 0.9 over a much wider range (+2 to +16 kHz) because it passes through the match faster.

from simpyson.templates import PulseSequenceTemplate


class HahnEcho(PulseSequenceTemplate):
    """90 - tau - 180 - tau - acquire on the first channel."""

    def get_default_parameters(self):
        return {
            "variable_pw": 2.5,
            "variable_rf": 100e3,
            "variable_tau": 100,
            "variable_tsw": "1e6/sw",
        }

    def get_required_parameters(self):
        return {"variable_pw", "variable_rf", "variable_tau", "variable_tsw"}

    def generate_code(self):
        return """
proc pulseq {} {
    global par
    pulse $par(pw) $par(rf) 90
    delay $par(tau)
    pulse [expr 2*$par(pw)] $par(rf) 0
    delay $par(tau)
    acq_block {
        delay $par(tsw)
    }
}
"""


echo = SimpCalc(
    pulse_spinsys,
    pulse_sequence=HahnEcho(tau=50),  # microseconds
    proton_frequency=400e6,
    spin_rate=10e3,
    start_operator="Inz",
    detect_operator="Inp",
    method="direct",
    crystal_file="rep100",
    gamma_angles=10,
    np=1024,
    sw=20e3,
    verbose=0,
).run()
print(
    f"Peak of the echo spectrum: {echo.spe['ppm'][echo.spe['real'].argmax()]:.1f} ppm"
)

Peak of the echo spectrum: 20.0 ppm

SIMPSON itself is the authority on what a pulse sequence may contain; see the SIMPSON papers and the dnp-grenoble/simpson examples for the available commands.

docs.title: Custom simulations with SimpCalc
docs.text:
SimpCalc builds a SIMPSON input file from a spin system, a pulse sequence and a set of simulation parameters, and can run it for you. Use it when simulate_spectrum() is not enough: a pulse sequence, cross polarisation, or your own Tcl.

Requires SIMPSON

Cells that call .run() need the simpson command on your PATH (see Installation). The outputs shown on this page were produced with SIMPSON 6.1.4 and are not re-computed when the documentation is built. Building and printing an input file never needs SIMPSON.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text: A spin system, a pulse sequence name and the simulation parameters. .print() shows the SIMPSON input that was generated, .run() runs it and returns a Simpy object.

docs.title: What SimpCalc needs
docs.text:
SimpCalc has no defaults for the simulation parameters. It raises a ValueError listing any that are missing when the input is generated.

Parameter Unit / values Meaning proton_frequency Hz (e.g. 400e6) 1H Larmor frequency; sets the field. Pass a number, not '400MHz', the value is written to SIMPSON unchanged. spin_rate Hz MAS rate (0 for static). start_operator e.g. Inz, Inx, I1x Starting density matrix. detect_operator e.g. Inp, Inc, I2p+I3p Detected operator. np points Number of acquisition points. sw Hz Spectral width. method e.g. direct, dsyev SIMPSON propagation method. crystal_file e.g. rep100, rep2000 Powder average. gamma_angles integer Number of \(\gamma\) angles. verbose integer or bit string SIMPSON verbosity (0 is quiet).

Optional output settings:

Parameter Default Meaning out_name temporary name Output file name without extension. out_format 'spe' 'spe', 'fid' or 'xreim'. lb 20 Exponential line broadening in Hz. gauss_lb 0 Gaussian line broadening in Hz (skipped if 0). zerofill np Zero-filled size; equal to np means no zero-filling, use e.g. 2*np to interpolate.

Other keyword arguments are written into the par block as they are, so you can add SIMPSON parameters or your own. Parameters whose names start with variable_ are written as variable entries.

What you can do with the calculator:

Call Result calc.print() / str(calc) Show the complete input file. calc.save("name.in") Write the input file to disk, e.g. to run it on a cluster. calc.run() Run SIMPSON and return a Simpy object. Temporary input and output files are deleted afterwards. calc.run(filepath="name.in", delete_files=False) Keep the input and output files. calc.run(read_output=False, delete_files=False) Return SIMPSON's printed output instead of a Simpy object. With the default delete_files=True the output file is deleted, so there would be nothing left. calc.run(dry_run=True) Write the input file and return the command, without running it. The file is kept. calc.run(simpson_path="/path/to/simpson") Use a SIMPSON executable that is not on your PATH.

If SIMPSON fails, run raises a RuntimeError that contains SIMPSON's error message.

docs.title: Example: the effect of the contact time in CP
docs.text:
In cross polarisation, magnetisation moves from an abundant nucleus (I) to a dilute one (S) through their dipolar coupling. The coupling between spins I and S depends on their distance \(r\):

\[b_{IS} = -\frac{\mu_0 \gamma_I \gamma_S \hbar}{4\pi r^3}\]

It falls off as \(1/r^3\), so nearby atoms couple strongly. The spin system below has one 1H coupled to two 13C with different couplings:

Pair bIS (Hz) Relative distance H-C2 -10 000 closer H-C3 -5 000 further

A short contact time transfers magnetisation only to the strongly coupled carbon; a longer contact time also reaches the weakly coupled one.

docs.title: Custom pulse sequences
docs.text:
For anything the templates do not cover, pass your own SIMPSON Tcl as pulse_sequence. The Tcl is the body of the pulse sequence: you write the SIMPSON commands, and SimpCalc wraps them in

proc pulseq {} {
    global par
    ...your code...
}

Parameters you want to vary go in the code as $par(name) placeholders. Give each one a value as a keyword argument; SimpCalc writes it into the par block as variable name value. Here a single pulse of length pw (µs) and power rf (Hz), followed by acquisition:

docs.title: Ramped versus flat contact
docs.text:
Many pulse sequences already exist online as SIMPSON input files. The example below is taken from dnp-grenoble/simpson repository that contains several experiments for recoupling, decoupling, cross polarisation and more.

To use one, copy its pulseq procedure and any helper procedures into a string, replace fixed numbers by $par(...) placeholders, and give the values as keyword arguments.

The example below is adapted from its ramped cross-polarisation (cross_polarisation/rampcp.in): the proton power is ramped from ramp_start to ramp_stop percent during the contact. Because the code starts with proc pulseq, the helper procedure ramp can be defined next to it.

A flat contact only transfers well when the rf powers match a Hartmann-Hahn condition, \( u_1^{\mathrm{H}} - u_1^{\mathrm{C}} = \pm n\, u_\mathrm{r}\). Here \(|60 - 70| = 10\) kHz is equal to the spin rate, so \(n = 1\). A ramp sweeps the proton power through the condition, so it also works when the nominal power is off, as long as the match lies inside the swept range.
